A name, an address, and a reason to hurry.
Black coffee and a cigarette on somebody else's tab.
Somebody wrote down what they should have burned.
A press photograph of the lobby, taken before the first uniform arrived.
A café check for two coffees at a quarter past one, signed E.S.
The vault log: box one-fourteen, opened by R. Voss at ten to midnight.
A cab chit, market to the Bluff at twenty past two, and the driver still on the rank.
The operator's log: the last call from suite eleven-hundred, at eight minutes to two.
The inventory of her effects: a bent ring, a brass key stamped one-fourteen, and no money.
A house photograph of Vera Lang on the Jade Room stage at eleven.
An import manifest: forty crates of orchids, and twelve of them signed for at night.
The poisons register: four ounces of ether, signed out by Doctor Pike at ten.
An unclaimed locker tag, and a wet coat with another tag in the pocket.
The union dues ledger, every line in Brandt's hand.
A customs report: a seal broken and a crate gone, with cart tracks leading out of the yard.
An unfinished letter from Lillian to her brother about the will.
The keeper's log: a lantern on the cliff path at half past two, and again at five to three.
A death certificate with drowning struck through and the truth written over it, forty minutes later.
The manifest Customs sat on for six weeks, with a second set of initials added at midnight.
The wireless log: stop at the usual place, understood, and at twelve past three, all done.
A pawn ticket for a rigging knife, redeemed the night before by somebody who did not pledge it.
A letter from the widow's husband, written in 1941 and kept seven years.
The chandler's sales book: forty feet of line and a sailmaker's needle, signed B.O.
The union account: four hundred dollars out on the tenth, signed by the vice-chair.
A radiograph of the wound: under the ribs and upward, from below.
A locker tag, an unclaimed oilskin coat, and a key to the bond store sewn into the lining.
A net tag from the Marie-Louise, found in the water off Pier Nine.
A coastguard fix on a rowing boat with no light: one man to Pier Nine at a quarter past eleven, one man back at ten to twelve.
A tide table with low water on the 12th marked in pencil.
Bask's café tab: tea every morning for twenty years, and a last line about a note he wrote.
The Canon's wine account, and a note about a returned cheque.
The crypt ledger with a page razored out tonight, and a fingerprint in the glue.
A photograph of the key board with the tower hook empty, and the verger in the doorway.
Constance's letter to the Dean, sealed and never posted, found in Blake's own desk.
The poisons book: chloral for Marrow House, signed by the Matron on the eighth.
The depot sheet: car seven out at a quarter to midnight, signed Fay, back at ten to one, wet.
The valve key book: key three out at ten to midnight and back at three with the wrong initials.
The crypt fund: four hundred pounds gone, one signature on every slip.
A photograph from the water tower: iron rungs on the outside of the bell tower, the bottom one bright.
A left-hand glove, grey kid, left on a chair after words at four in the morning.
A diocesan report with the plates of the tower torn out in the shop doorway.
The Lamplighter's slate: wet boots, two rums, and a man who said he had rung it and laughed.
The storm boards were not moved. Somebody went through a ten-inch gap as it stood.
A hundredweight of salt came down the lane on one shoulder, and the man scraped both gate posts.
Blood on the underside of the lamp bracket, seventy-six inches up, where a head caught it.

The boat cover reeks of sweet smoke. Somebody sat under it with a pipe.
Two hours in a boat in February, and not a bottle, not a butt, not a card.
The salt sack stinks of cheap shag tobacco, and he never smoked it.
Orchid perfume on his collar, strong enough to come through the sea water.
A thumb print on the ladder rail, and it is in machine oil.
The thread from the pockets smells of ether. It came from the hands that pulled it.

The trapdoor frame is split at shoulder height, and it took weight to do it.

A pale hair in the cut end of the rope, fair as winter straw.
One red hair in the rust on the fourth rung. Copper, and not out of a bottle.
Five grey hairs in the cut end of the rope, and none of them is hers.
The rope fibres are laid over right to left, from a blade drawn in the left hand.
One blow from behind, landing on the left side of her head, swung from the right hand.
Under her nails, skin and blood and a fleck of old scar tissue.
A boy under the tower saw a hand on the rungs with blue ink on the wrist.
A hand print in chalk on the ringing-floor rail, and it has four fingers. Only four.
The boy saw the face in the lamp for a second, and there was nothing on it.
A marker from the Lamplighter's back room, lying in the chalk by the trapdoor.
A hip flask of brandy on the stair, a third gone, and she did not drink.
The curtain on the ringing floor reeks of sweet smoke. Somebody waited behind it with a pipe.
An hour waiting on the ringing floor in February, and not a bottle, not a butt, not a card.
The sally of the rope stinks of cheap shag tobacco, and she never smoked.
Orchid perfume on her veil and collar, and the convent allows no scent.
A thumb print on the top rung, and it is in machine oil.
The cut end of the rope smells of ether. It came from the hand that held it.
A neat size eight, both feet, where they dropped from the bottom rung into the mud.
A size ten in the mud under the rungs, worn hard on the outer heel.
A size twelve in the mud under the rungs, toes toward the reservoir.
Rear window,
Rear sash found raised nine and one-quarter inches and jammed there on a frayed cord. Paint scuffed along the inside edge of the sill and a thread of dark wool caught on the catch.
No damage to the frame and no tool marks: the sash was not forced any further than it stood. Whoever came through it came through it as it was.
Corridor door,
Door frame split along the jamb at fifty-eight inches from the floor on the strike side. The split is fresh and runs outward, consistent with a shoulder driven against the frame from the corridor.
No tool marks. The lock held; the wood did not. It takes weight to do this to oak.
Preliminary findings,
Arterial spatter on the north wall arcs from a point of origin no lower than seventy-four inches from the floor. The deceased stood five foot four in stockings.
The assailant faced her and stood over her, and the blow was delivered downward from well above her head.
Trace examination, item 1
Not the deceased's: hers is dyed auburn and shows it at the roots. This one has never seen a bottle. Caught in the setting when the ring hand was raised.
Lifted from the inside of the collar, which means a head was close over hers. The deceased's hair is dark; nobody on the hotel staff is fair.
One red hair on the pillow, and nobody else in the building with a head like that. Copper, unmistakable, and not out of a bottle.
Trace examination, items 1–7
Pulled out in the struggle, by the roots. The deceased was twenty-six and had not a grey hair on her. These came off the other head in the room.
A single blow to the right temple. The track runs downward and toward the left side of the skull, entering at some thirty degrees from the front.
Bruising on her left forearm where she raised it. The assailant stood square in front of her when the blow was struck.
Trace examination, item 3
Powder residue on the outer index finger and the web of the thumb, consistent with a small-calibre discharge. The interior is worn through at the fingertips: an old glove, and the working one.
Trace examination, item 5
She marked whoever she fought. Among the fresh tissue under her nails is a fleck of old scar: fibrous, pale, years healed. She scratched somebody who had already been cut once.
Statement of the night lift attendant
"The hand came down on her shoulder and the cuff rode up. There was ink on the wrist. Blue. A picture, not letters — something with a curl to it."
"I did not see a face. I see hands all night; I could not tell you a face if you paid me."
Plate 4: tumbler, sideboard
Print lifted from the dust on the sideboard where the tumbler was set down. Palm and four fingers, clear. Not a partial: the surface is clean where a fifth finger should have rested.
Statement of the night clerk
"Ordinary. That is what I keep telling you. Nothing on the face, nothing on the hands, no mark I could point to. You could not pick them out of a line of ten."
"I would know them again. I could not tell you why."
Pencilled chit
"I.O.U. $40 — Wed. — Rosie's." Creased in half, stepped on, and dropped in the struggle. Nobody who does not play carries a marker from Rosie's.
Plate 2: two glasses, the table
Two glasses. Hers has the lipstick. The other has a ring of rye still in it and a thumbprint we cannot match. The deceased kept no rye in the suite; somebody brought their own.
Trace examination, item 8
Somebody in that room smoked a pipe that was not tobacco, and recently. The soot at the sill is from a small lamp. The deceased did not use; her doctor is emphatic.
Inventory,
Whoever spent the evening here left nothing of a habit behind, because they have none. In this city that is rarer than a fingerprint.
Trace examination, item 6
The curtains and her lapel are saturated with it. The deceased did not smoke, and the hotel sells Turkish. Somebody stood close to her for a long time with the cheap stuff on their coat.
Orchid, laid on thick and transferred by contact. Not hers: she wore jasmine and nothing else. Somebody stood very close.
Plate 6: brass push-plate, corridor door
A thumbprint in machine oil on the brass. Somebody who works with machines and never quite gets it off, whatever they scrub with.
Trace examination, item 7
Faint, sickly, hanging over the pillow. Hospital ether, which nobody buys in a shop.
Cast no. 1, flowerbed below the window
A neat impression pressed into the flowerbed, the heel narrow. Shallow, too: not a heavy tread.
Cast no. 1, the yard
A plain sole, worn down hard on the outer heel: somebody who walks a great deal and walks badly.
Cast no. 1, wet ash by the back stair
Pressed deep into the wet ash by the back stair. Twelve inches even, and a heel like a brick.
In a dead man's handwriting
Folded four times and soft at the creases. "If anything happens to me —
The rest is water.

Somebody put it on their tab and did not leave a name.

Lobby, the Gilded, 2:40 AM
Taken before the first uniform arrived. Perpetua Shaw in the foreground, notebook out, hat off. Something about her in the flash that you would not have noticed by lamplight.
On the back in grease pencil: HOLD FOR MORNING.
Check no. 2207
Two coffees, one drunk. Signed to the house account in a hand the waiter knows.
The second cup was still warm when the chair emptied.
Access log, box 114
11:50 PM — R. VOSS — box 114 — signed out 11:58. The signature is hurried and the pen dug through the page.
Miss Vine remembers the hand that signed, and what it looked like doing it.
Fare chit no. 88
The driver is still on the rank outside, and he knows a way up the Bluff that is not on any map.
Calls placed from the Gilded, suite 1100
12:52 AM — outgoing — LANTERN 4-4 — duration one minute ten. The last call the suite ever made.
Quill wrote the number down when she should not have.
Effects of the deceased, Voss, L.
A brass key stamped one-fourteen in the pocket of a woman with no purse to spend. The morgue does not guess what it opens. You are allowed to.
The eleven o'clock spot, Nov. 3
Vera Lang on the little stage at eleven, in the flash. The house photographer sells these at the door for a dollar. This one was not bought; it was taken.
You can see a great deal of a person in a flash photograph.
Consignment, SS Marseillaise
Forty crates, orchids, Marseille to Ashgrave. Twenty-eight initialled at the dock by the bond clerk. Twelve initialled by somebody else, in the importer's own hand, at the warehouse, at night.
She signed for them herself. The clerk remembers the hand.
Entries, Nov. 3
10:05 PM — ether, four oz. — signed A. PIKE — purpose: "surgical". The signature is his, the chemist says, and the hand that made it he has watched a thousand times.
Tag no. 9
A coat, wet through, hung in locker nine at half past two and never claimed. In the pocket, a second locker tag from somewhere else in the city.
Collections, week of Nov. 3
Every entry in Brandt's hand, and every hand that paid him remembered by the man who keeps the book. He knows more about the collector than the collector knows about himself.
Seal broken, bay 4
A crate went out without paper, and the cart tracks in the wet lead out of the yard and up the road.
To Roland, unfinished
"Rollo — I have changed the will and I have told Father's lawyer why. When you read this you will already know. I am sorry it had to be me who—"
The pen stops. The rest of the page is clean.
Lights on the Bluff, night of Nov. 3

2:30 — lantern on the cliff path, stops at the old stair, returns. 2:55 — lantern again, further out. 3:10 — nothing. The keeper thinks it was the fishermen. You will have to go and look to be sure it was not, and it costs you an hour to find out it was.
Certificate of death, Bask, A.
Signed twice by the same hand forty minutes apart. The first entry is written in a hurry and struck through with one line. The second is written slowly.
Kite, the attendant, notes in the margin that the doctor stood with the body for the whole forty minutes in between and did not speak.
Manifest, SS Corvina

Six weeks of crates, every page initialled by the inspector and not one crate opened. A second set of initials has been added over hers tonight, in a different pen, by somebody who knew her initials but not her hand.
Traffic, night of the 11th
Three messages, logged in the operator's hand, the last one underlined twice.
Ticket no. 3391
Okafor's knife, pledged in March so he could eat, and bought back the night before the murder by a stranger with Okafor's ticket in his hand.
To Tilda, 1941, never sent
"If I end up in the water it was not the water. Ask Bask. He knows who on this boat wants me gone, and he will be at the wheel. — A."
Kept seven years in a drawer, read so often the folds have gone soft.
The 11th, evening
The last sale of the day, at closing. The chandler signed for it himself, which he never does, and the apprentice watched a stranger's hand rest on top of his while he did it.
Longshoremen's Local, account 40
One withdrawal in a year of deposits, two days before the vote, with the purpose line empty.
Plate 2: right side, the deceased
The blade entered under the right ribs and travelled upward toward the heart. Whoever held it was below him, on the ladder or in a boat, looking up.
Tag no. 17
The coat was never collected. The man who left it ran when the attendant found the key.
Tag, net 6, MARIE-LOUISE
A brass net tag, stamped for the Marie-Louise, fished out of the water under Pier Nine at low tide by the man who found the body. The Marie-Louise carries no nets.
Fixes, 11:15 PM and 11:50 PM
Bearings taken from the tower and plotted. The rowing boat went under the pier and came out again thirty-five minutes later.
February, spring tides
A pencil mark against low water on the 12th. That is when the pier gave him up. Nothing else on the page.
A. Bask — twenty years

Tea every morning for twenty years at a penny a day, paid every Friday. The last line, in Nell Mott's hand: "10th — sat with D.H. an hour, argued about a name. Wrote a note on my paper and took it with him."
Account, the Rectory, April
Twelve of sherry, six of port, and a note from the merchant: "Canon — the crypt fund cheque was returned again. We must ask." Mrs. Tull has watched him drink the twelve.
Interments, 1939

Plot forty-four: a name, a date, a fee of forty pounds, and the page it was on razored out tonight. The stub is still in the binding, and Miss Pym knows which page it was because she gave it to Constance last week.
Whoever cut it left a fingerprint in the glue.
Plate 3: the verger's key board

Forty hooks, thirty-nine keys, and the empty hook labelled TOWER in the verger's hand. In the flash, the verger himself, caught in the doorway, and something about him the constable did not notice at the time.
To the Dean, unposted

"...I must therefore report that Mr. Blake has been seen with the boys of the third form at the Observatory after lights out on three occasions, and that Dr. Quint has declined to say what they were shown. — C. Ayre." Sealed, stamped, never posted, and found in the desk of the man it names.
Entries, April
Chloral hydrate, two drachms, signed S. CRAKE, for Marrow House, the 8th. Miss Lamb watched her sign, as she has watched her sign every month for eleven years.
Sign-out, night of the 9th
Car 7 — out 00:02 — R. FAY — back 00:51 — "wet". The dispatcher did not sign it and does not know how she got the key. He watched her bring it back, and what she did with her hands while he asked.
Valve keys, the 9th

Key 3 out at 23:50 against the Canon's standing order, returned 03:00 with initials that are not his. The walkway it opens runs along the top of the reservoir wall, and the wet prints on it run one way.
Crypt restoration fund
Four hundred pounds gone from a box with one signature on every slip. Constance had asked to see the box on Thursday. On Friday she was dead.
Plate 9: the bell tower, from the water tower

Taken at dawn with a long lens: the tower, the stair window, and on the outside of the tower a line of iron rungs the diocese had forgotten about, running from the ringing floor to the ground. The bottom rung is bright where the rust has been worn off tonight.
One glove, left hand
A woman's glove, left hand, grey kid, left on a chair after words at four in the morning. Mrs. Petty saw the hand that took it off. She also saw the hand it belonged to, and the difference.
Diocesan Report, 1939, plates I–IV

The plates show the crypt, the tower, and the outside of the tower with its iron rungs — the only photograph anyone has of them. Torn out in the doorway tonight and carried off. What is left is a caption: "Rungs to be removed, 1940." They were not.
Amsel knows who bought it and will save you the walk.
Tonight
Rudge chalks what the hill owes him. Tonight: "wet boots, two rums, no coin, said he had rung it and laughed." No name. You will lose an hour finding out it was the drunk who says that every night.
Storm boards,

The pier ladder is boarded over for the winter. The only way down to the water is a ten-inch gap between the third and fourth boards, and somebody went through it tonight: the edges are rubbed clean of weed, and a thread of dark wool is caught on a nail head.
Not one nail is lifted. The boards were not moved. Whoever went down to the boat went through the gap as it stood.
Gate, the lane from the salt works to

A sack of rock salt, one hundred and twelve pounds, was carried down the lane on a shoulder and no cart. Both gate posts are rubbed white with salt at fifty-six inches: the sack scraped one side and the man scraped the other.
A man has to be as wide as the gate to touch both posts at once.
Lamp bracket,

The underside of the lamp bracket at the ladder head carries a smear of blood at seventy-six inches. Somebody stood up under it with a wet hand and caught the iron with the top of the head or the hood.
The deceased stood five foot nine. The smear is above where he could have reached standing, and he was not standing.
Effects examination, item 3
Sewn right through by the needle, so it was on the sewing hand when the pocket was closed. The deceased is grey. This hair has never been grey and never seen a bottle.
Twisted into the thread itself, which means it was on the hand that pulled the stitches tight. The deceased is grey and nobody on his boat crew is fair.
Lying on top of the salt inside the pocket, so it went in with the salt. Copper, and not out of a bottle. There is not a head like it on the deceased's side of the harbour.
Effects examination, items 3–8
Six grey hairs sewn through the seams, from the sewing hand. Compared under the glass with the deceased's own: his are coarse and nearly white; these are finer and darker grey, and they are not his.
Post-mortem,
A single wound under the right ribs. The track runs upward and across to the deceased's left, toward the heart. The assailant was below him, facing him, on the ladder or in a boat.
A knife driven upward from below and across to that side is a knife in the left hand.
Effects examination, the pockets

Both pockets sewn shut with the same over-and-over stitch, worked from right to left with the knot finished on the right. That is how a right-handed man sews sailcloth: needle in the right hand, cloth held in the left, the work moving toward the left.
A left-handed man sews the other way, and finishes on the other side.
Scrapings, both hands,

The deceased got a hand on whoever was below him. Under the nails of the right hand: skin, blood, and a hard white fleck that is old scar tissue, the kind that comes away from a badly healed wound when it is clawed.
Statement of a ferry hand, aged fourteen

"There was a boat under Pier Nine with no light. A hand came up and took hold of the ladder rail, and the sleeve went back, and there was blue on the wrist. Ink. Like the navy men have. I didn't see a face. I saw the wrist."

Nettie Roe. I keep the morgue register and I wash the bodies. The bodies are easier.

Cyril Dunn. I'm the chemist. I fill the prescriptions. I don't ask what they're for, and I don't forget who asked.
A customer. I've handed them their little bottles across this counter.

Lulu Fane. I've worked this bar since Lillian sang here. I remember who came to listen to her and who came to watch her.

Pete Vasko. Every car on the Bluff comes through my garage. Tonight one came in with the front wing smashed.

Hugh Latimer. Every crate in this warehouse has a customs seal, and every seal has my initials on it. Tonight one of them has somebody else's.
They sign my book. You notice the hand that signs.

Milo Denk. I run the ferry. Last crossing is at one-forty. I don't know names, but I never forget a face I've seen after midnight.

Mr. Voss argued with his sister at ten. He left at eleven with only one cufflink in.

Suite 1100 rang down for ice at midnight. At nine minutes past two, Mr. Halloran, the house detective, went up with a passkey because the light was on and the door was on the chain. He came back down white as a sheet.

Staff. Mr. Strand. Guests who don't want to be seen. It locks from the inside. Tonight it was open from one o'clock until I locked it at three.
The door was on the chain?

From the inside. Mr. Halloran had to cut it. So whoever killed her didn't leave by the door. The bathroom window gives onto the fire escape, and the catch was open. Nobody on the eleventh floor opens that window in February.
What was Miss Voss like?
Kind to the staff, hard on everyone else. She tipped in silver and remembered your name. She remembered too much about everybody, I think.
Vera finished at one and went straight out the front door. She had her coat on before the clapping stopped.
Brandt came in at eleven and left at half past. He was going to Rosie's card room. He goes every Thursday and every Thursday he says he doesn't.
Dr. Pike drinks here when he can't be seen drinking on the Heights. Rye, doubles. He wasn't in tonight.
Did anything happen here tonight?
Vera did two sets. A man came in white as a sheet, went out the back, and came back looking lighter. Somebody left a matchbook from Rosie's on the bar, and nobody admits to going to Rosie's.
Vera left in a hurry. Where did she go?
She said home. But she took the tram up to the Heights. Her home is the other way.
Did Lillian Voss drink here?
She sang here first, before the Jade Room and the Gilded. She came back once a month, sat at the end of the bar, and didn't sing. She was here on Tuesday.
Dr. Pike stitched a man's hand at three in the morning and let him walk out. Left hand, cut on glass. Pike didn't write the man's name down. I did. It wasn't a real name.
The Deacon visits her brother on the second floor every Sunday. She pays his bill in cash and cries in the corridor afterwards.
Roland Voss was on my ward in March for his nerves. He talked in his sleep about his sister.
What came through the hospital tonight?
A cut hand at three. A drunk at four. And at half past two, a telephone call asking if we had a patient called Voss. We didn't. Not yet.
Who called about a Voss?
A woman. She didn't give her name. It sounded like she was calling from a bar; there was music.
What do you keep in your notes on Dr. Pike?
Dates and amounts. Ether by the pint. I'm not a policeman. I write things down in case one ever turns up.
Madame Mireaux was on the wharf at two with a lantern and a cart, waiting. She never carries things herself. Tonight she did.
Brandt lifted a crate into a boat at half past two, on his own. It had taken two men to lift it off the cart.
What did you see tonight?
A crate going from a cart into a boat. A woman with a lantern. And something small thrown off the end of the pier that didn't sink.
Where did the boat go?
Across the bay, toward the Bluff, with no lights. There's only one place under the Bluff where you can land a boat without lights.
Did Lillian Voss ever come to the docks?
On Wednesday. She stood right where you're standing and watched the crates come off the boats for an hour. She wrote in a little notebook. She didn't need to talk to me.
The Deacon's light was on in the vestry until midnight. Then it went off. It came on again at three. In between, she wasn't in there.
Miss Shaw sits at the back of the church and watches who takes communion. Then she writes it down.
Who was in the church tonight?
The Deacon, on and off. And a man in the vestry at one o'clock who wasn't the Deacon. He left by the side gate. I didn't see his face. I saw a hat.
What did the man in the vestry want?
The letters. Miss Voss had written to the Deacon. The letters were in the vestry drawer. They aren't there now.
Did you know Miss Voss?
She gave to the soup kitchen and she counted the collection plate. She was the only person on the Heights who ever counted. That's why she's dead, if you ask me. Nobody has.
Miss Lang pawns a bracelet every month and buys it back the week after. Tonight she bought it back early.
Madame Mireaux doesn't pawn. She buys. Whatever the docks lose, she has by Friday.
Mr. Strand pawned a gold lighter with his initials on it in June. He never came back for it. Somebody else did.
What came through the shop tonight?
One ticket paid off in cash at midnight, by a hand that hadn't pawned the item. One bracelet bought back early. And a man who looked at the knives for a long time and didn't buy one.
Who bought back Strand's lighter?
A woman in gloves. She paid with a new banknote and didn't wait for her change. She went up the street toward the Jade Room.
Tell me about the man who looked at the knives.
Big. Quiet. Hands like shovels. He looked at the knives the way a man looks at something he already owns.
Mr. Voss left at eleven with only one cufflink in and a face like a wet Sunday.
Miss Lang sat in the cheap seats on Tuesday and cried all through the second act. It was a comedy.
Miss Shaw takes box D on Thursdays so she can watch the Voss family in box C.
The Voss box was empty from eleven o'clock. A coat was left over the rail. A woman came for it at half past one, in a hurry, wearing gloves.
Whose coat was it?
A man's camel coat. Expensive. The woman who took it wasn't the woman who came in with him.
Did Miss Voss come to the theatre?
Every Thursday, in box C, her father's old seat. Last Thursday she came alone and left at the interval. She looked at me on her way out as if she wanted to say something. She didn't.
Mr. Strand has coffee with a lady who isn't Mrs. Strand, Tuesdays and Thursdays. Tonight he left without finishing his coffee.
The doctor takes his coffee black. His hands shake until the second cup.
Mr. Voss comes in after the theatre and drinks brandy out of a coffee cup. He thinks I don't know.
Who was in here tonight?

Mr. Strand and his lady at a quarter past one. He left at twenty past as if something had bitten him. She stayed and drank both coffees. Then at three, a big man in a wet coat came in, ordered nothing, and watched the door.
Who is Strand's lady?
I pour coffee. I don't ask names. I know she wears a wedding ring and turns it round and round when he's late.
Tell me about the man in the wet coat.
Big. Hat pulled down. He asked if the tram to the Bluff was still running. It wasn't. He walked.
The Deacon walks in the park when she can't pray. Tonight she walked from midnight until two.
Young Mr. Voss sat on the bandstand steps on Tuesday, drank from a flask, and talked to nobody.
Miss Lang cuts through the park to get to the Gilded. The railings on the north side are loose. She knows it.
Who came through the park tonight?
The Deacon, walking. A man sitting on the bandstand at one, waiting. And a woman climbing over the north railings at half past one, running.
Tell me about the man on the bandstand.
Hat down over his face. He didn't smoke. He waited an hour. Then a woman came from the direction of the Gilded and they walked off together toward the Trust bank.
Did Miss Voss walk here?
Every morning at seven with a book. Not a novel. An account book. She read account books the way other women read novels.
Mr. Voss signed for box 114 at ten to midnight. His hand shook so badly the pen went through the paper.
The Deacon pays two hundred pounds a year into an account in her brother's name. Cash, in small notes.
Madame Mireaux has accounts here under three different names. All of them are hers.
Who came to the vault tonight?
One person. Mr. Roland Voss, at ten to midnight. He had a key that wasn't his and a signature that was.
Did Miss Voss come in on Tuesday?
Yes. She put an envelope into box 114 and took nothing out. She told me: if my brother comes, let him. He needs to see it. So I let him. I shouldn't have.
Did Miss Voss bank here?
Since she was twelve. She counted the money after the teller counted it, every single time. She was never wrong, and she never apologised for checking.
Miss Shaw telephones the Herald from hotel lobbies at all hours. Tonight she called from the Gilded at a quarter past two. Before the police had been called.
Mr. Strand gets a call every Thursday at one o'clock from a woman on the Heights. Tonight the call came and he wasn't at the desk to take it.
Dr. Pike telephones his pharmacy at midnight most nights. Tonight he telephoned the docks instead.
What calls did you connect tonight?
All of them. At 12:52 a call went out from suite 1100, Miss Voss's room, to the number Lantern 4-4. It lasted a minute and ten seconds. That was the last call ever made from that room.
Whose number is Lantern 4-4?
It's the telephone by the bar at the Jade Room. Somebody there took a call from a woman who was about to die. I listened in. I shouldn't have. She said: I know what you did.
Did she telephone anyone else this week?
Everyone. The Trust bank. The Herald. Mercy Hospital. The pharmacy. A shipping office. She was ringing round the whole city like a woman settling her accounts.
Brandt rides my tram standing up at the back, so he can see everyone. Tonight he rode the last car up the Heights at one, and the last car down at a quarter past two, and got off at the docks.
The Deacon rides to Marrow House on Sundays and comes back with red eyes.
Miss Lang got on at the Parrot at one and got off at the Heights. Her home is down in the Flats.
Who rode the last tram?
Eleven passengers. A singer going the wrong way for home. A big man who got off at the docks. And somebody who got off at the wrong stop and walked back.
Tell me about the one who walked back.
Coat collar turned up. Got off at the Trust bank and walked back down the hill toward the Gilded. I punched the ticket but I didn't see the face. I saw good shoes.
Did Miss Voss ride the tram?
Never. She had the family car. Except on Wednesday. On Wednesday she rode down to the docks with me and stared out of the window the whole way, as if she was memorising it.
Miss Shaw reads her own old columns here. Twenty years of them. She's looking for something she wrote and forgot.
Dr. Pike came in on Wednesday and asked for the Herald from 1946, the cannery fire. He read it twice and put it back upside down.
Who was in the reading room tonight?
One man, at midnight, with a razor blade. He cut a page out of a 1946 newspaper and left. The page was about the cannery fire.
Which way did he go?
Toward the Trust bank. He had ink on his fingers. Not printer's ink. Fountain-pen ink.
Did Miss Voss read here?
Every Thursday afternoon for six months. Old newspapers, account books, the shipping registers. She was building a case against somebody. I don't think she finished it.
Dr. Pike came down at four to see her. He touched her hand and said her name. Then he asked to see her personal effects. I said no.
Mr. Voss came at five. He didn't go in. He stood in the corridor and asked me whether she had suffered. I lied.
What did she have on her?
A ring, bent out of shape. A brass key stamped 114. An orchid stem. No handbag, no money. Somebody took the bag and left the key. So they didn't know what the key was for.
The ring was bent?
Bent at the setting. She hit somebody with it. There's a hair caught in it that isn't hers.
Who came to see her?
The doctor at four. The brother at five. And at six, a woman who wouldn't give her name. She stood outside the door for ten minutes and then left. Gloves. Perfume.
Dr. Pike signs the poisons register himself now. He never used to. He started in September.
Madame Mireaux buys nothing here herself. She sends a boy. The boy signs with a cross.
Miss Lang buys something for her throat every week and something for her nerves every month.
Who came in tonight?
A man at midnight, for bandages and iodine. One hand was shaking and the other was cut. He paid in silver and didn't want a receipt.
Show me the poisons register.
Here. Ether, four ounces, Thursday, signed A. Pike. He has signed for eleven pints this year. There isn't that much surgery on the whole of the Heights.
Did Miss Voss come here?
Once, on Wednesday. She asked to see the register. I showed her. She copied a page into a little notebook and thanked me. I've been waiting ever since for somebody to come and ask me about it.
Vera had a drink here at half past one, still in her stage dress with a coat over it. She'd been crying. She said it was the rain.
Brandt sat by the door from half past midnight and watched the telephone. When it rang at eight minutes to one he took it himself, listened, and walked out without paying.
Emil Strand left his lighter on my bar at half past two. He didn't notice. He was watching the door.
The telephone rang at two o'clock.
It did. A man answered it. Big, in a hat. He listened without saying a word, put the receiver down, and walked out. He left a full glass on the bar. Nobody leaves a full glass.
Who was the man?

Not a regular. He came in at half past twelve and sat where he could see the telephone. He was waiting for it. When it rang at eight minutes to one he took it, listened, said nothing, and left without paying.
Lillian used to sing here.
For three years. She was better than this room deserved. She came back in October, sat at the end of the bar, and told me she was going to burn the whole Heights down. I thought she meant a song.
Young Mr. Voss brings the Packard in with a new dent every month. Tonight it was the front wing. He said he hit the gate. He didn't hit a gate.
Brandt doesn't drive. He gets driven. Tonight somebody drove him from the docks up to the Bluff at a quarter to three in a car that wasn't his.
Tell me about the Packard's wing.
Smashed in on the passenger side, about hip height. There was paint in the dent. Not gate paint. Black paint. That car hit something painted black, and hit it hard.
What was in the glove box?
A woman's glove. Just one. Grey leather. Too small to be Miss Voss's, I'd say.
Who drove it in?
Not Mr. Voss. A man in a chauffeur's coat who didn't know where the headlight switch was. Anyone who drives that car every day knows where the switch is.
Madame Mireaux signs for twelve crates a month herself. I asked her why. I've stopped asking.
Brandt took a crate out of bay four at half past two in the morning without any paperwork. I wrote it down. He watched me write it down.
Mr. Strand takes delivery of two crates a month at the hotel. The paperwork says orchids.
Customs seal 4471 was broken tonight.
At half past two in the morning. By Brandt, on Madame Mireaux's orders. The crate went onto a cart, the cart went to the docks, and then a boat. After that I stopped watching.
What's in the twelve crates?
Not orchids. Orchids don't weigh that much. I opened one in September. I closed it again. I have a family.
Miss Voss came to the warehouse.
On Wednesday. She read the manifest standing up and asked me whether I had ever opened a crate. I said no. She looked at me as if she knew I was lying. I was.
Madame Mireaux takes the last ferry every Thursday with a suitcase and comes back on Friday without it.
The Deacon takes the ferry to Marrow House on Sundays. She sits at the back and doesn't look at the water.
Who was on the last ferry?
Nine people. A woman with a bundle. A man in a wet coat. The bundle went over and didn't come back. The man went over and didn't come back either.
Tell me about the woman with the bundle.
Gloves. Perfume so strong you could smell it over the diesel. She carried the bundle up toward the manor as if it was a baby. It wasn't a baby.
Did Miss Voss ever take the ferry?
On Wednesday, to the Bluff. She stood at the rail the whole way and asked me what the boats without lights were. I said fishing boats. She said they weren't.
The Frenchwoman's boats land under the Bluff with no lights. I write it in the log. Nobody reads my log.
Brandt came up the cliff path at three with a lantern and went back down without it.
What did you see from the lighthouse tonight?
A boat with no lights at two o'clock. A lantern on the cliff path at half past two, stopping at the old stairs. And the manor: every window lit at three, and every window dark by four.
What's at the old stairs?
A cave. Dry inside. The smugglers used it before the lighthouse was built. Somebody uses it now.
She came up the tower on Wednesday and asked to see my log. She read three months of it, said thank you, and went down the stairs as if she was counting them.
Emil Strand rents out the hotel's ninth floor by the hour. He thinks nobody knows. Lillian knew.
Dr. Pike gives half the rich people in this city their pills. He gave Lillian hers too.
Roland is a sweet boy who owes money to people who are not sweet.
Perpetua Shaw wrote that I sang flat. I didn't. She wanted my job for a friend of hers.
Brandt drinks at the Parrot and never pays. Nobody dares ask him to.
Cass Mireaux sends flowers to people who never ordered any. Ask yourself why.
The Deacon takes money from the church collection. Everyone in the Flats knows. Nobody on the Heights does.
Where were you at two this morning?
On stage at the Blue Parrot until one. Two encores. Then a cab home, and bed. Ask Bix, the barman. He'll tell you.
What was Lillian to you?
A friend, first. Then my boss. Then the woman who got me fired from the Jade Room over a dress. We were going to make up. We were always going to make up.
Your set list says she owed you the top spot on the bill.
She promised me the top spot in July. Then she got the Gilded job and forgot all about it. I underlined it because I was angry. It doesn't mean anything more than that.
Somebody used the hotel's side door at half past one. Was that you?
A long silence. Yes. I went to ask her for my old job back. She laughed at me. I left. She was alive when I left, Inspector. She was laughing.
If it wasn't you, then who?
Somebody with a key. That side door locks from the inside. I only got in because it was open, and it was open because somebody was expected.
Miss Lang came in through the side door at half past one. I saw her from the balcony. I didn't stop her.
Dr. Pike keeps a room on the ninth floor. I don't ask what for.
Roland Voss argued with his sister at ten o'clock. The whole floor heard it.
Miss Shaw spends more nights in this hotel than she does at home. Never as a paying guest.
Brandt collects union money in my lobby. I let him. It's cheaper than not letting him.
Madame Mireaux sends the orchids every Monday. The bill goes to the Voss family.
The Deacon collects from my staff every Friday. She keeps half of it, I'm told.
At the front desk. Miss Pruett will confirm it. I was at the desk from midnight until six.
Lillian found your book of room bookings. What was in it?
Names, times, room numbers. Half the city council. She said she would never use it. She said it like somebody deciding when.
You have a key to every door, including the side door.
I have the master key. So does the house detective. And until Tuesday, so did Miss Voss. She asked me for one. I gave it to her. I don't know why she wanted it.
Two coffees at Café Belvedere at one-fifteen, signed with your initials. You said you were at the desk.
His face goes grey. I stepped out for twenty minutes. Miss Pruett covered for me. If you need to know who the second coffee was for, I'll tell you somewhere with a door that shuts.
The orchid was put back in its vase. Who tidies up in this hotel at two in the morning?
Nobody. Whoever did that has stood in a lot of hotel rooms and left them looking as if nobody had been there.
Miss Lang has a sore throat I've treated and a temper I haven't.
Strand sends me patients. I send him a cheque. That's the whole arrangement.
Roland Voss has been my patient since he was nine. Bad nerves. He never grew out of them.
Perpetua Shaw wrote about my pharmacy once. I haven't slept properly since.
I stitched Brandt's hand in 1946. He didn't flinch. Men who don't flinch worry me.
Madame Mireaux imports flowers. I'm a doctor. That's all I know about flowers.
The Deacon's brother is in Marrow House asylum. I signed the papers. She has never forgiven me for being right.
Asleep at home. Then at Mercy Hospital at three, stitching up a man's hand. The admission slip is there. Read it.
Lillian was your patient. What were you giving her?
Nothing she shouldn't have had. Something to help her sleep. I signed for it. It wasn't enough to hurt her, and she never tried to take enough.
She was going to name your pharmacy in court.
She said so, on Wednesday. She had the poisons register, or a copy of it. I'd like to know where she got it as much as you would.
You signed out four ounces of ether on Thursday.
For an operation that didn't happen. The patient never came. The ether is still in my bag. I can show you. I'd rather you didn't ask what else is in the bag.
Whose hand did you stitch?
A man who gave no name and paid cash. Left hand, cut on glass. He'd been somewhere with a lot of broken glass.
Vera Lang wants what Lillian had. She has wanted it since she was nineteen.
Strand rents rooms to men who buy my flowers for women who aren't their wives.
Dr. Pike is a customer. For flowers.
Roland Voss owes money at my dock. I don't collect it myself.
Shaw came to my warehouse in October asking about crates. I gave her orchids. She went away.
Brandt moves what I need moved and doesn't ask questions. I like that in a man.
The Deacon buys lilies for funerals on credit and pays for them out of the collection plate.
At the bonded warehouse, counting crates. Latimer, the clerk, saw me. He always sees me.
The orchid on her dressing table came from you.
Every orchid on the Heights comes from me. I sent that one on Monday. Somebody snapped it. Somebody who has no idea what they cost.
Twelve crates on your manifest are signed in your handwriting, not the clerk's.
A very long pause. The clerk was ill. I signed for them myself. That isn't a crime.
'Don't let her see the manifest.' That's a telegram from Marseille with your name on it.
Then you already know she saw it. She came to the warehouse on Wednesday and read it standing up. She said nothing at all. That was worse.
Did you give her a silk scarf?
Yes. Orchid-scented. She wore it for a month. Then she gave it back, on the day she read the manifest.
Miss Lang sings in a club I don't go to. She sings well. I've heard her through the wall.
Mr. Strand puts money in the plate every Friday. Guilt money. It spends the same.
Dr. Pike had my brother committed. He was right to. I'll never say that to his face.
Roland Voss sits in the family pew and watches the door.
Miss Shaw comes to Mass to see who else does.
Nikolai Brandt gives to the soup kitchen every week. In cash. Nobody knows where it comes from.
Madame Mireaux sends lilies for every funeral in the parish. She knows about most of them before I do.
In the vestry, praying. Old Wyn will tell you the light was on.
Lillian wrote to you about the parish accounts.
She did. And she was right. Two hundred pounds a year, for nine years, for my brother in Marrow House. I was going to confess to the Canon on Sunday.
Your hymn book was found on the bandstand steps in the park, with an orchid petal pressed inside it.
She stops. I was in the park, not the vestry. I walk when I can't pray. I found the petal on the path and kept it. I don't know why.
Who did you see in the park?
A man on the bandstand, in a hat. He sat there for an hour without smoking. That's how I knew he was waiting for somebody.
Vera was Lil's real friend. They fought like sisters. I should know.
Strand let me into her suite once when I lost my key. He didn't ask why.
Pike has had a hand in my pocket since I was nine. Pills, advice, bills.
Shaw wrote that I cried in the wrong order. How does anyone cry in the wrong order?
Brandt collects debts for men I owe money to. He's polite about it. That's the frightening part.
The Frenchwoman lent me money in the spring. Lil paid it back. I never asked how much.
The Deacon buried our mother. She was kind then, and she's kind now. It's exhausting.
At the manor, in bed. The driver brought me home at midnight. He'll tell you so. He always tells you so.
You argued with her at ten o'clock.
About money. It was always about money. She said she was changing her will. I said some things. I walked out. That was the last thing I ever said to her, and it was a bad thing.
Her safe-deposit box was opened at ten to midnight. By you.
He puts his hands over his face. I wanted to see what she'd done. I took the new will. I haven't read it. I can't.
The family car came into the garage at ten to three with the front wing smashed.
I hit the manor gate. At midnight. I'd been drinking. That's all it was.
What does the will say?
I don't know. I told you. It's in a drawer, and I look at the drawer.
Vera sings. I listen. She never sings the one I ask for.
Strand pays the union to keep the hotel quiet. Every month, on time.
Pike stitched my hand once. Good hands, bad eyes. He never looked at my face.
The Voss boy owes forty dollars at Rosie's card room. I collect for Rosie. I haven't collected yet.
Shaw wrote about the union once and got it right. I didn't like that.
The Frenchwoman pays cash and doesn't talk. Best kind of work there is.
The Deacon feeds my mother's whole floor every Thursday. I give what I can.
At the union hall, counting dues. Four men saw me. If you want their names, you can have them.
Your four men were at Rosie's card room. So were you.
He looks at the floor for a long time. Fine. Rosie's until one. Then the docks. Then home.
What were you doing at the docks?
Moving a crate for the Frenchwoman. Off a cart and into a boat. I didn't open it. I never open them.
There's a threatening letter on union paper nailed to the cannery door.
I don't type. Somebody at the hall does. Somebody who wants the cannery to think it came from me.
You send money to your mother on Tenement Row.
Every week. She thinks it's union wages. It isn't always union wages. Leave her out of this.
Vera Lang sang flat in July. I wrote it. She's never forgiven me for being accurate.
Strand's ninth floor is the best-kept secret on the Heights. Which means I've known for years.
Dr. Pike keeps a poisons register that would ruin him. Lillian had a copy. I'd give a lot to know where it is.
I wrote that Roland cried at the wrong moment. I meant it kindly. It didn't read that way.
Brandt is the only honest man in the union. He's honestly dangerous.
Cass Mireaux gave me orchids to stop me asking questions. I took the orchids. I kept asking.
Iris Tovar takes from the collection plate. I've known for two years. I haven't printed it. Ask me why.
You were in the lobby before the police. How?
A bellboy telephoned me. I tip bellboys. That's my whole profession.
The photograph shows you in the lobby at two-forty with your hat off. You'd been there a while.
I'd been in the building since one o'clock. On the ninth floor. With somebody. If you print that, I'll print you.
Your column that morning was about her.
My column every morning is about somebody. Alive, she was the best material in the city. Dead, she's a month of columns, and I hate every one of them.

Gone from her suite, I'd guess. If I had them, you'd be reading them in tomorrow's paper and I'd be on a train out of town.

No. Not for you, not for the Commissioner, not for God. Ask me anything else.

You have no right to that. She—. She changed the will. I took it. I have not read it. I could not.

Yours. It was on the Jade Room bar at two. You said you were at the desk.
I was not at the desk. I was at the Belvedere. With someone. If it comes out, she is finished. So am I.

Emil Strand. Two o'clock, near enough. He had his hands round a glass like it might get away.
A matchbook from Rosie's, half the matches gone.
Rosie's. Who plays there?
Brandt. Every Thursday, and he loses. He was there Thursday. He lost big.

I was at Rosie's. Then I was at the docks moving a crate for the Frenchwoman. Ask the watchman. Ask what was in it. I never did.

It is Lillian's scarf. I gave it to her. She gave it back the night she found the manifest. She said she did not want anything of mine near her.

Lillian's. She wore it the night she had me fired. Whoever had it last had it at the baths. Lillian never went to the baths.
A cufflink under the dressing table, engraved R.V.
Yours. Found under her table.
I was there at ten. We argued. I left at eleven. Dot Bell saw me leave the Lyceum after, alone. I did not go back. I swear to God I did not go back.
Roland Voss. When did he leave?
Eleven. Alone. He had one cufflink in. I notice cufflinks. He did not come back for the second act.
A pocket watch on the manor stairs, stopped at eight minutes to two.
One fifty-two. That was the call from the suite.
It was. One minute ten. She said one thing and hung up. She said: I know what you did, and I am telling them tomorrow.
The watch stopped at one fifty-two. You were her doctor. What stops a watch?
A fall. Or a hand that closes on it. Ether does not stop watches, Inspector. Ether stops people.
Ashgrave Bay. Salt and Silence.

Aurel Bask, head of the dockers' union, was found under Pier Nine at low water. Stabbed once from below, his pockets sewn shut and filled with rock salt. That is a warning to anyone who talks. He was going to make a speech on Thursday about smuggling through the trawler berths. The union votes on Thursday. Nobody in the harbour talks to police.
Inspector, this is Dunmore at Harbour Station. A fisherman found a body under Pier Nine at low water this morning, about ten to five.
It is Aurel Bask. Head of the longshoremen's union for twenty years. Every docker in this harbour knew him, and most of them were afraid of him.
He was stabbed once, under the ribs, from below. Then somebody sewed his coat pockets shut, filled them with rock salt, and put him in the water. His watch stopped at twenty to midnight.

The salt is a message. In this harbour it means: this is what happens to a man who talks. Bask was going to make a speech on Thursday about the trawler berths and the smuggling everybody pretends not to see.
The union votes for a new boss on Thursday. Customs has been sitting on a ship's manifest for six weeks. A trawler called the Marie-Louise went out last night with no cargo and came back heavy.
Nobody down there talks to police. Do not go to Pier Nine alone and do not go in uniform. You have until the vote. Start with the body at the morgue, or with the people who saw him last.
Aurel Bask
Harbour Station. Do not go to Pier Nine alone. Do not go in uniform.
The union votes on Thursday. Every candidate is on your list.
Customs has sat on a manifest for six weeks. Lean on them.

You make the arrest at the Hall an hour before the vote, in front of three hundred longshoremen who go quiet all at once. Somebody at the back starts clapping and thinks better of it. The tide comes in. It always does.

Thursday comes. They elect a new boss. The new boss says all the right things about Aurel Bask. The salt goes in an evidence locker. The file goes in a drawer. The harbour goes back to being a place where nobody saw anything.

Ruth Gault. I log the boats. In, out, weight, captain. When the log and the water disagree, I write down what the water says.

They sit in that hall every Thursday. I've swept around their feet for years.

Émile Delacroix. I set the type for the union newspaper. I know every word before the union does, and I know who wanted which words changed.
They bring me their articles. You learn a person by what they cross out.

Femi Oyelaran. I've guarded these crates for six weeks. In six weeks nobody came for them. Until tonight.
They come to look at the seals. You learn a person by how they look at a seal they aren't allowed to break.

Nan Mott. Tea is a penny. For another penny I'll tell you who drank it. Bask drank his tea here every morning for twenty years.
They take tea here. I've set a cup in front of them a thousand times.

The kettle's off. So am I.
Aldo Penrose. I polish the brass plaque and read out the names of the drowned. There's a new name on it this week, in chalk. I didn't write it.
They come to the plaque. You learn a person by which name they touch.

Jean Sable, Coastguard. I log every boat that crosses the Narrows after dark. I also know which ones aren't in the log.
They pass under my telescope. You learn a person by how they stand at a wheel.

The watch changes at six. Ask somebody else.
Nurse Ives. I run Dr. Fenn's wards. I run them better than she runs her paperwork.
They've been through my ward. You don't forget a patient. Or a visitor.

I'm doing my rounds. If you're not bleeding, out.
Bram Cully. I cut the ice and stack it. A trawler unloaded at my steps at three this morning, and afterwards a man sat in my cold room with his hands in the ice.
They buy ice from me. You learn a person by what they need to keep cold.

Ice doesn't wait. Neither do I.
Ma Lundy. Everything in this harbour ends up in my shop window sooner or later. On the 10th something went out of it that I wish I had kept.
They pawn things with me. I look at their hands.
A pawn ticket was paid off on the 10th, in cash, by somebody who wasn't the person who pawned the item. They went toward
The shop is shut. I've said more than I should.
Tamsin Rook. I'm the conductor on the last tram along the quay at midnight. I punch the tickets, and I remember the people who'd rather I didn't.
They ride my tram. You learn a person by where they refuse to sit.
Somebody rode to the end of the line at half past nine and didn't ride back. Later I saw the same coat going toward
The tram's in the shed. So am I.
Jack Orme. I bag salt. A hundredweight a bag, six hundred bags a night. Tonight I'm one bag short.
They come here for salt. You learn a person by how much they can carry.
The missing bag went out on somebody's shoulder at ten. That somebody walked down the lane toward
The kilns need feeding. You don't.
Sam Cotter. I found him. I was under the pier at low water for the crab pots and there he was, face down, heavy as a church.
I see them on the water. You learn a man by how he handles a boat.
The tide took something off him before it gave him up. It fetched up along the shore near
I've said it three times now. I need to sit down.
Brother Fry. Forty beds and a stove. I count the men in at ten and count them again in the morning. The numbers don't always match.
They sleep here sometimes. You learn a person by what they say in their sleep.

The men are sleeping. Keep your voice down and go.
Dov came in at a quarter past midnight with his flask and sat until one. He wasn't celebrating. He'd lost something. Money, I think.
Ledoux doesn't drink here on the nights he sails. He wasn't here. He was at sea, or wherever he goes instead.
Mrs. Rask hasn't set foot in this pub since 1941. Sometimes she stands outside. I leave the door open.
Who was in on the 11th?
Forty men who saw nothing. Bask on his stool from half past ten. Hollis with his flask from a quarter past midnight. Nobody who mattered in between.
Tell me about Bask's last hour here.

He drank one stout and didn't finish it. At a quarter past eleven he stood up with a folded note in his hand and said: Mags, I have a boat to meet, and if I don't come in tomorrow, look at who does. I laughed. I'm not laughing now.
What was on the note?
I didn't read it. It was café paper, the Dockside's, folded in four. Nell Mott's paper. Ask her who wrote on it.
Miss Wren left at eleven. Her initials on the manifest were dry. At midnight there were new initials, and they were wet, and they weren't hers.
Mr. Salvi comes to the Customs House once a month and leaves an envelope. I copy manifests. I don't copy envelopes.
What happened here on the 11th?
Miss Wren left at eleven. At midnight somebody let themselves in with a key and added initials to the Corvina manifest. They looked like hers. Close enough for a judge. Not close enough for me.
Whose ink was it?
A fountain pen with a broad nib. Miss Wren uses a fine one. The only broad-nibbed pen I know of in this harbour is on the desk in the shipping office.
Did Bask come here?
On the 9th. He read the manifest at my desk and copied it into a little notebook. He asked me if I'd ever opened a Corvina crate. I said I was only a clerk. He said: so was I, once.
Mr. Okafor signed for the rope himself. A man had his hand on top of Mr. Okafor's hand. I saw it from the back of the shop.
Salvi's crews buy the good rope, pay cash, and never come back for the same length.
The doctor bought a scalpel from us last month. She said the hospital had run out. I didn't believe her.
What did you sell on the 11th?

Forty feet of thin line and a size fourteen sailmaker's needle, at closing time, eight o'clock. That's for sewing a coat, not a sail. The buyer paid double to keep it quiet, and Mr. Okafor signed for it himself with the buyer's hand on top of his.
Describe the buyer.
An oilskin with the hood up. He never looked at me once. He smelled of fish and ice, and half this harbour does. Mr. Okafor knew him. I could see it in his neck.
Did Bask buy from you?
Every week. On the 10th he bought a padlock. A big one, for the union hall's back office, he said. Somebody got into that office anyway.
Dr. Fenn wrote 'drowning' at twenty to six and went and stood with him. She came back at twenty past with her hands washed and wrote the truth over it.
Mrs. Rask came at a quarter to six and asked to see him. I let her. She looked at his pockets and nodded, as if something had been confirmed.
Tell me about the body.

A fisherman found him under Pier Nine at low water, ten to five. I had him here by a quarter past. Pockets sewn shut with sailcloth thread and a size fourteen needle. Rock salt in them, about a hundredweight between the two. The wound is under the ribs, going upward. Whoever did it was below him, on the ladder or in a boat.
Who came to see him?

The doctor at half past five, and she stayed an hour. The widow at a quarter to six. And at half past six a man in an oilskin who stood in the corridor with his hands in his pockets and wouldn't come in. He was crying. He went toward the slip.
Tell me about the salt.
Rock salt from the salt works, the coarse grade. A hundredweight of it. Somebody carried that to the pier on his shoulder without a cart. That's a strong man, or a desperate one.
The skipper took the dinghy to Pier Nine alone and told me to wait. I smoked the whole time. He never lets me smoke on deck. That night he didn't notice.
Hollis came down to the boats once, in 1946. He was seasick tied up at the quay. Bask laughed at him.
The lighthouse keeper watches us land. He waves. Then he goes inside and writes.
What did you see from the deck?

We anchored in the Narrows at ten past eleven with the lights off. The skipper took the dinghy to Pier Nine at a quarter past to fetch a passenger for Salvi. He came back at ten to twelve alone, wet to the waist, and said the passenger hadn't shown. Then we went out to the Corvina.
Wet to the waist.
He said he'd slipped off the ladder. He sat in the bow all the way out and didn't say another word. And something went over the side off the pier before he rowed back. A sack. It floated.
Where did the sack go?
With the tide, toward the salt works. It washed up on the outfall pipe. It had the works' stencil on it, and it was empty.
What's in the hold?
Nobody has ever told me. I've smelled it. It isn't fish. It's whatever the cannery cans when there aren't any fish.
Miss Wren bathes on Tuesdays and cries in the steam room where she thinks nobody can hear.
Mrs. Rask hasn't been in since 1941. Her husband bathed here every Friday.
Garrow comes down from the lighthouse once a month and sits in the hot room like a man trying to boil something off himself.
Who came through the baths?

A man in an oilskin at half past four in the morning, wet to the waist, with his hands wrapped in a rag. He wanted the hot room and wouldn't take a towel. He left his coat in locker seventeen with something sewn into the lining.
What was sewn in the lining?
A key, stamped 'Bond Store 12'. He ran when he saw I'd found it. He ran toward the Narrows, where the trawlers tie up.
Did Bask bathe here?
Every Friday for twenty years. On the 10th he sat in the hot room and told me the union was about to find out what it had been carrying. I thought he meant the dues.
Miss Wren's stamps and my log should agree. Since the Corvina came in, they haven't once.
Salvi declares his cargo weights the way some men declare their age.
Garrow and I keep the same log from opposite ends of the harbour. Mine is honest. His is crossed out.
What moved on the 11th?

The Marie-Louise out at eleven with no cargo declared. Back at five past three, sitting low in the water, at the ice house steps and not her berth. High tide at 1:40. I wrote 'low?' with a question mark. The question mark is mine.
Sitting low with what?
Corvina cargo, for the ice house. Ask the ice man what came off her. Ask the lighthouse keeper what he crossed out.
Bask came to this office.
On the 9th. He read six weeks of boat movements and copied every Marie-Louise entry into a notebook. He said: Ruth, you've been writing it all down. I said somebody had to.
Garrow has no wireless. He doesn't need one. He has a lamp and a grudge.
Salvi's messages are all about fish, and not one of them ever names a fish.
Ledoux taps a key slowly and heavily, like a man who doesn't want to be understood.
What went over the wireless?

At 1:04, from the shipping office to the Marie-Louise: STOP AT THE USUAL PLACE. At 1:06 the reply: UNDERSTOOD. At 3:12, from the Marie-Louise: ALL DONE. I underlined that last one twice, because I know what it usually means, and tonight I'm not sure I do.
Where is the usual place?
The ice house steps. Every boat that lands without Customs lands there. Ask the ice man what came off her tonight, and who.
Did Bask send anything?
On the 10th, to the union's city office: ONE MORE THING TO CHECK, THEN I NAME THEM. I sent it. I haven't slept since.
Dov left at midnight with the committee. He was the last to sign the minutes and his hand was shaking.
Mrs. Rask has had a key to this hall since 1941. Nobody ever took it back. She has never used it.
Bernard came to the hall on the 10th to beg Bask for more time. Bask gave him a week. He didn't need a week.
What happened at the hall?

The election committee until midnight. Then quiet. Then at one o'clock somebody opened the back office with a key that wasn't the vice-chairman's, and left with Bask's little notebook. There was mud on the floor from a woman's heel. Small. Neat.
What notebook?
The one he wrote the boats down in. He kept it in the back office behind a new padlock. Whoever has it has the whole harbour in their pocket. The heel prints went out toward Customs Row.
Twenty years. What was he like?
He never once sat down in this hall. He stood at the back like a man who didn't expect to be allowed to stay.
Hollis came in at five past midnight and pulled the chairman's notice with his own key. He said the chairman had changed his mind. His hands were shaking.
Mrs. Rask places a notice every year on the anniversary of her husband's death. This year she placed it early.
